citations.short_gloss: Earliest English provincial glossary witness of the goyster/gauster/goster ('to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud') verb family (< ME galstren).
citations.source_publication: Ray, John, A Collection of English Words Not Generally Used, with their Significations and Original, in two Alphabetical Catalogues, 1st ed. (London: Printed by H. Bruges for Tho. Barrell, 1674), p. 67.
citations.page_and_column: Title leaf n0 ('1674'); South and East Countrey Words, p. 67 (leaf n80)
citations.verbatim_quote: Gods good: Yeaſt, Barm. Kent, Norf. Suff. To Goyſter: to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud, Suff. Gowts, Somerſets. Canales, cloacæ, ſeu ſentinæ ſubterraneæ.
citations.linguistic_note: Establishes the seventeenth-century English dialectal verb stem underlying later northern and Midland gauster/goster (consonant skeleton KSTL, matching the second constituent of snollygoster with zero consonant-skeleton edit distance). In subsequent editions of Ray's Collection (including the 1737 third edition, North Country Words, p. 32), the northern vocalism is explicitly cross-referenced as 'To Gauſter; as Goyſter', descending from Middle English galstren ('to make a boisterous noise, cry out') with regular pre-sibilant l-vocalization.
citations.analysis_notes: Red-Team blind scan verified on John Ray's 1674 first-edition London title leaf (n0, 'Printed by H. Bruges for Tho. Barrell ... 1674') and p. 67 physical ink (leaf n80). Patched Pass 1's punctuation in verbatim_quote from 'laugh aloud. Suff.' to the printed comma 'To Goyſter: to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud, Suff.' (preserving long-s 'ſ') and uploaded an unclipped corrective WebP scan. MCP phonological scoring confirms goyster (consonant skeleton KWSTL) is chronologically plausible more than a century and a half prior to the 1845 American debut of 'Snolly Goster', representing the southern/East Anglian diphthongal sibling of northern gauster/goster (KSTL).

scan.rights_note: Published 1674 (on or before Dec. 31, 1930); in the United States public domain. WebP proof scan hosted in R2.

citations.short_gloss: Eighteenth-century British provincial documentation pairing North Country 'GAUSTER' with Kentish 'GOYSTER' and participial 'goyſtering'.
citations.source_publication: Grose, Francis, A Provincial Glossary, with a Collection of Local Proverbs, and Popular Superstitions, 1st ed. (London: Printed for S. Hooper, 1787), sig. E4v & Supplement, sig. *K3r.
citations.page_and_column: Title leaf n9 ('M.DCC.LXXXVII.'); Main Glossary, sig. E4v (leaf n72, s.v. GOYSTER); Supplement, sig. *K3r (leaf n157, s.v. GAUSTER)
citations.verbatim_quote: GAUSTER. See GOYSTER. [Main Glossary, leaf n72:] GOYSTER. To laugh aloud. Kent. A goyſtering laſs or girl, a romp, or tomboy.
citations.linguistic_note: Pairs the northern back-vowel stem gauster (consonant skeleton KSTL, identical in consonant structure to goster and the -goster termination of snollygoster) with southern goyster and agentive-participial goyſtering ('a romp, or tomboy'). GAUSTER), and a corrective WebP scan was uploaded removing a stray 'N.' caption in Panel C1. MCP phonological scoring confirms gauster (KSTL) matches the four-consonant right-hand constituent -goster of snollygoster (SNLWKSTL).

citations.short_gloss: Yorkshire West Riding 'GAUSTERING' ('Imperious, boasting'), documenting the shift from noisy laughter to overbearing braggadocio.
citations.source_publication: Carr, William, The Dialect of Craven, in the West-Riding of the County of York, with a Copious Glossary, 2nd ed., Vol. I (London: Printed for Wm. Crofts, 1828), p. 177.
citations.page_and_column: Vol. I title leaf n7 ('1828'); Glossary, p. 177 (leaf n193)
citations.verbatim_quote: GAUT, A male or castrated pig. Su. C. gallt. Isl. gallte, porcus. GAUSTERING, Imperious, boasting. GAUVE, To stare vacantly. GAUVEY, A dunce. GAUVISON, A silly, staring fellow.
citations.linguistic_note: Captures the exact semantic bridge required for American frontier 'Snolly Goster' (1845) and later political 'snollygoster' (1855/1895): in West Riding Yorkshire speech, gaustering (base skeleton KSTL) denotes 'imperious, boasting' behavior rather than mere laughter, matching the bombastic self-magnifying rhetoric of the ring-tailed roarer and stump politician.
citations.analysis_notes: Red-Team blind scan audit verified Wm. Crofts's 1828 second-edition Vol. I title leaf (n7, '1828') and p. 177 physical ink (leaf n193, confirming 'GAUSTERING, Imperious, boasting.' and the 1828 compositor's printed 'Su. C. gallt.'). Caught a critical framing defect in Pass 1's R2 scan (which boxed and zoomed 'GAUMLESS / GAUP' four lines too high, omitting 'GAUSTERING') and uploaded a verified corrective WebP proof scan via upload_proof_scan. Precedes the October 1845 Ohio Valley debut of 'Snolly Goster' by seventeen years and documents the West Riding Yorkshire semantic shift from noisy laughter to imperious boasting.

citations.short_gloss: South Yorkshire (Sheffield/Hallamshire) monophthongal spelling 'GOSTER' ('to boast, to bully, to hector') sixteen years prior to 1845 'Snolly Goster'.
citations.source_publication: Hunter, Joseph, The Hallamshire Glossary (London: William Pickering, 1829), p. 45.
citations.verbatim_quote: GOSTER, to boast, to bully, to hector:—Yes, to hector, which can only mean to act like Hector: but how could our ancestors so misunderstand that beautiful character, in which modesty is not the least conspicuous feature, as to give currency to such a profanation of it,
citations.linguistic_note: Records the exact <o>-spelled northern English dialect verb goster (/ˈɡɒstə(r)/, 'to boast, to bully, to hector') sixteen years before 1845 'Snolly Goster', supplying a plausible formal and semantic ingredient for the compound's second element without directly documenting its coinage.
citations.analysis_notes: Red-Team blind scan audit verified William Pickering's 1829 first-edition title leaf ('MDCCCXXIX.', leaf n6) and p. 45 physical ink (leaf n76), patching Pass 1's normalized terminal period to the 1829 compositor's actual printed comma at the close of the entry ('such a profanation of it,'). MCP phonological scoring confirms standalone goster (1829, skeleton KSTL) is chronologically plausible sixteen years before 1845 'Snolly Goster' and matches the four-consonant second element -goster of snollygoster (SNLWKSTL) exactly (leaving only the four-consonant first element SNLW- outside the simplex verb) while delivering the exact '<o>' spelling and 'boast, bully, hector' semantics echoed in 1841 Ohio Valley 'goster'.

citations.short_gloss: Dialectal 'goster' ('boisterous bragging talk') in a New Orleans Picayune stage-Irish dialogue reprinted in Georgetown, Ohio four years before 'Snolly Goster'.

citations.verbatim_quote: Former President Truman may have been making a talknophical assumnacy when he said that snollygoster is what Southerners call a man born out of wedlock. Experts of the Dixie dialect rushed to their dictionaries .... They reported that a snollygoster can mean a number of things, including tadpoles and politicians. But they didn't find Truman's definition in their research.
citations.linguistic_note: Notes that snallygaster appears in print decades after 1845 snollygoster ('there is little evidence to suggest an etymological relationship'), discusses Pennsylvania German 'schnelle geeschter' ('quick spirits'), quotes both the Oct. 25, 1866 Foster item and the Jan. 25, 1890 Buffalo Morning Express 'snolly-goster men' verse, and points toward British dialectal 'goster' as a plausible source.
citations.analysis_notes: Verified live URLs on Merriam-Webster Wordplay and Grammar. Calibrates both ends of the monster question: chronology weakens the traditional derivation of 1845 snollygoster from 1909 snallygaster without by itself proving reverse borrowing.
